page_title: A humble guide to database schema design

sources.entry: A humble guide to database schema design, Mike Alche

summary.title: A humble guide to database schema design
summary.one_liner: Learn practical database schema rules: aim for at least third normal form, use constraints as a safety net, split addresses and names into separate fields, and keep consistent naming conventions.
keywords: store full address in one field
first name last name separate columns
takeaways: Good schema design preserves information and reduces redundancy to avoid update inconsistencies.
Aim for at least third normal form: store atomic values and avoid transitive dependencies between non-key columns.
Use foreign keys, NOT NULL and CHECK constraints as a last line of defense for data quality, and define ON DELETE/ON UPDATE behavior.
Split addresses into fields like street, city, state and postal_code, and store first and last names separately.
Pick a consistent naming convention, such as underscore-separated lowercase names, and stick to it.
summary.summary: The article argues that good database schema design matters for scaling applications and gives five guidelines: use at least third normal form, add constraints as a last line of defense, never store full addresses or first and last names in a single field, and establish consistent naming conventions. It explains first, second and third normal form with worked table examples showing redundancy and update or deletion anomalies. It also covers practical trade-offs, such as how a name split can still be imperfect for names with particles or multiple surnames. The tone is informal and example-driven, with PostgreSQL constraints referenced via a link.
